1:
Every voice begins by admitting the obscurity. Clarke calls this the most difficult prophecy in the Old Testament, difficult to us because we know neither the king nor the people intended, though he is satisfied they were well known when the prophet wrote. Henry says the critical expositors have enough to do to enquire them out, and declines either to add to their observations or to determine their controversies, offering only that the first name seems to be the king and the second the kingdom.

The identifications are many, and Clarke and Gill between them list most of them. Clarke reduces the probable candidates to two, a king of Persia or a king of Syria, and reports Calmet, whom he calls one of the most judicious commentators that ever wrote on the Bible, declaring for the former. He reports also that Mede supposed the Americans were meant, as colonies of the Scythians; that Houbigant declared for the Scythians themselves; that Kimchi understood the Christians and Turks; and that a pastor at Utrecht concluded for the Syrian king alone, since the name signifies covered and answers to what historians describe of his character. Gill adds an early Latin father who thought of the Goths that ravaged the Roman empire, and those who take the name as a common title for the kings of the lesser Asia and Syria, strengthened by finding in Pliny that a city of Syria was called by its own people Magog. Wesley refuses a single person, though he allows that one may be pointed out by whom the troubles began, and holds that all the enemies of Israel, open and secret, may be intended.

Ellicott argues from the genealogy of the nations, where the second name stands in connection with the Cimmerians and the Medes. Early Jewish tradition, adopted by Josephus and Jerome, identifies them with the Scythians, a view probable to nearly all modern expositors; but the name must be understood geographically rather than ethnologically, of the tribes living north of the Caucasus. Driven from their original home, they had poured down upon Asia Minor and Syria shortly before the time of the prophet, advancing even as far as Egypt, and were finally driven back, leaving their name a terror to the whole eastern world for their fierce skill in war, their cruelty and their rapacity. It was probably the memory of these recent inroads, Ellicott suggests, that led the prophet to select their name for the powers hostile to the Church of God. On the first name he notes that it was generally supposed to be formed from the second by dropping a syllable, until an Assyrian inscription was found naming a Scythian chief which one scholar identifies with it.

Gill and Henry read the placing of the prophecy. Gill ties it to what came immediately before, the restoration of the people and their settlement in their own land, so that this predicts a disturbance they should meet for a short time from a powerful enemy; Wesley says God forewarns them what enemies and troubles would interpose before he would fully deliver them. Henry notices the order within the chapter itself: the confusion of the enemy is put first, and God turns him back and puts hooks in his jaws before it is foretold that he will be brought against the land, so that the people had assurance of deliverance before any prospect of danger. So tender is God of the comfort of his people, Henry says, and so careful that they may not be frightened, that even before the trouble begins he tells them it will end well. Keil and Delitzsch supply the outline of the whole: the invasion by the appointment of God in the last times, the intention of plundering a people dwelling in security, and the wrathful judgment by which the nations shall know that God is the Lord.
3:
The turning back is the first crux. Gill will not have it of a repulse: God does not put hooks in the jaws to send the enemy home, as he put a hook in the nose of the king of Assyria and brought him back from Jerusalem, but uses him in providence to draw him out of his own land into Judea, as fishes are drawn with the hook out of the water; he compares the drawing of Sisera and his army, citing Kimchi and Ben Melech and the Targum. Clarke reads the clause the other way in four words, that the enterprise shall fail. Ellicott allows that turning back is the more common meaning but says that even so it cannot mean turning back from the holy land; taken with the figure of the next clause it would mean turning the wild beast away from his natural inclination to the fulfilment of the purpose of God. He prefers the sense of leading astray, and notes that in the Revelation this leading astray of the nations is ascribed to Satan, just as one book makes God and another Satan move David to number the people, God being said to do what he allows to be done. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion from the form of the verb, which may mean either to cause to return or to lead away from the right road, and take it here of enticing to a dangerous enterprise, with the Chaldee agreeing.

The muster of nations is read either as geography or as symbol. Gill identifies each name in turn with the modern map, taking the whole confederacy for the auxiliaries of the Turks: a neighbouring kingdom that will be confederate with them, a second which he refuses to place among the Abyssines and puts instead in the Arabia that lay between Judea and Egypt, and a third named after a son of Ham who, according to Josephus, founded it, whose inhabitants the Targum calls by his name and in whose direction a river of the same name runs. Gomer he takes for the people the Greeks called Galatians, descended from the eldest son of Japheth, or else for Phrygia, either way in the lesser Asia. Clarke reads the same names as the auxiliaries of a Syrian king, noting that one country was tributary to him and that a prophet names two of the others at his steps, and follows Calmet in identifying the northern pair with the Cimmerians and Turcomanians. Wesley gives the equivalents shortly and adds the more northern peoples. Ellicott refuses the whole approach. Having summoned the nations from the extreme north, the prophet turns to the east, then to the south and west, and names no neighbouring nation at all, but only those living on the confines of the known world; the supposition of a literal alliance of nations so situated, he says, is out of the question, and the address returning to the extreme north makes this a general gathering of the strength of the world against the Church of God.

The command to prepare is heard as irony by two. Gill says it is ironically spoken, suggesting that the enemy would indeed do so and yet all would be in vain and to no purpose; Wesley says God and the church deride this mighty preparation. Ellicott takes it straight: every preparation is to be made on the part of the invader and the nations, and then he himself is to be their guard, to control and guide the assault. Gill also notes that the titles at the opening are repeated for confirmation, and to show that all the greatness and grandeur and power they name would not protect their bearer from the vengeance of God.
8:
The visitation announced after many days is variously handled. Keil and Delitzsch defend the plain sense against those who would soften it: the word never means to be missed or to perish, as one interpreter supposed, and the sense of a penal visitation is to be retained. The objection that no punishment is in view until later loses its force, they say, once it is seen that visiting is a more general idea than punishing: the visitation consists in the fact that God leads the invader against the land in order to sanctify himself upon him by judgment. Ellicott reaches the same result another way. Various ingenious attempts have been made, with no great success, to give the words a different sense; the supposed difficulty arises from not observing that the whole course of the enemy is viewed as a single transaction. Not merely his ultimate destruction but the steps which led to it are brought about under providence and form part of the visitation, as one might speak of a whole career of sin as itself a visitation upon the sinner. Clarke reports two datings, one placing the fulfilment four hundred years later, the other placing an expedition against Egypt some twelve years after the return from Babylon.

How long the land had lain waste is pressed for evidence of date. Ellicott notes that the word rendered always means continually, and that the mountains had by no means been always waste, though during the captivity they were so constantly; yet the word is commonly used for a relatively long period, for which the captivity seems too short, so that it may indicate the later and longer dispersion. He observes too that the word for people is plural, marking a gathering back from many quarters. Wesley makes the many days the latter days of the kingdom of the Messiah, and reckons the waste from the carrying away of the ten tribes. Ellicott adds that the description of a people living in prosperity and security looks quite beyond anything hitherto realised in their history, and corresponds to the attack described in the Revelation.

The evil thought is where the two accounts of causation are reconciled. Ellicott notes that the leading of this foe against the Church has twice been represented as the act of God, and that here it is explained that God did this by allowing him to follow out the devices of his own heart. Gill makes the passage a proof of foreknowledge, since thoughts contingent and voluntary are certain to God, who knows them before they are conceived. Ellicott renders the phrase about the midst of the land literally as the navel of the earth, where position, unsuspecting security and riches combine to tempt the cupidity of the invader. Gill has the invader saying all this to his counsellors and generals and allies, to have their approbation and to encourage them to join him.

The three names that answer him are read as bystanders rather than allies. Gill insists they are not among those who come along on the expedition but neighbouring nations bordering on Judea who address him as he passes: the first two the Arabians of the parts nearest Judea, the third the Tyrians and Zidonians who traded by sea, or the merchants of Tartessus in Spain, which the Septuagint and Arabic versions render the merchants of Carthage. Wesley sets them at the compass points, one south, one east, one on the western sea-coast, and reads the young lions as young men thirsty of blood but more of spoil, who resolve to join if they may rob for themselves, their repeated question being an agreement to assist on condition of keeping what they seize. Ellicott takes the names as added to the earlier list to show that all the nations of the world sympathise in this attack upon the Church.
14:
The question put to the enemy is read two ways by Henry, who takes both. It may intimate his inducement: intelligence is brought him how securely, and therefore how carelessly, the people dwell, which gives rise to his project, since when he knows not only what a rich but what an easy prey they are likely to be, he will soon determine to fall upon them. Henry draws from this that the providence of God is to be acknowledged in the occasion, the small occasion perhaps, and that not designedly given, from which great enterprises take their original. Or the question may intimate his disappointment, since they dwell safely not in their own apprehension only but in reality, under the divine protection, so that he shall be made to know it by the fruitlessness of his endeavours, and shall find that there is no enchantment against Jacob. Ellicott simplifies the grammar instead, holding the passage clearer if the question is dropped and the words read that when the people dwell securely the enemy will observe it and come; Wesley reduces the clause to the same sense in six words.

The north remains the direction of the danger. Gill traces the origin to Scythia, or the Tartary that lies north of China, with peoples drawn from the Euxine and Caspian seas and the northern parts of the lesser Asia, and repeats his identification of the invader with the king of the north. Wesley names the same seas and countries. Henry, who places the enemy in Syria, notes only that this lay on the north of Canaan.

The sanctifying is agreed to be the purpose of the whole. Gill says the coming up is repeated for certainty, not for the comfort of the enemy but for his ruin, and not to the terror of the people but for the glory of God. Wesley reads the bringing as a permitting, and takes the sanctifying to mean that God shall be confessed a great God over all, gracious and faithful to his people and a dreadful avenger against the wicked, and that in the sight of the heathen who are with the invader and much more of his own people. Clarke fixes it on a particular defeat, that of the troops of a Syrian king under his general. Ellicott says only that the expression about the latter days is indefinite but concurs with the earlier ones in indicating a distant future.

The appeal to old prophecy divides them sharply. Clarke reports two datings once more, one holding that the prophecy concerning the Syrian king was delivered about four hundred years before the events, the other maintaining that the king of Persia is spoken of and referring to ancient prophecies in Isaiah. Wesley says simply that God has spoken of all these enterprises and will defeat them as surely as he foretold them. Ellicott makes the verse decisive against every particular identification. The interrogative form is one often used for emphatic assurance, and the statement is that God had of old and for a long time foretold this attack by his prophets; but the name is not mentioned in any earlier prophecy now extant, nor is it likely that any such, far less a long series of such, have been lost. This concurs with many other indications to show that the prophecy does not relate to any particular event, the enemy and his allies representing the enemies of the Church in general, and the prophet depicting the same prolonged struggle between the powers of the world and the kingdom of God which has formed the burden of so much prophecy earlier and later. Keil and Delitzsch translate what follows closely, with the wrath of God ascending into his nose and the sword called against him throughout the holy mountains, the sword of the one against the other.
18:
Keil and Delitzsch open with a dispute about whose words these are. Two interpreters held that the verses contain words God spoke through the ancient prophets, which this prophet now transfers to the enemy and to the time of his appearing; Keil and Delitzsch deny it. The perfect tense does not warrant the assumption, being purely prophetic and expressing the certainty of a divine determination as a thing clearly proved; nor can the formula of the preceding verse be taken as a preterite, nor these verses separated from what follows as a word long predicted and only now uttered. They explain the figure of wrath ascending into the nose from a psalm where smoke ascends in the nostrils of God, the outburst showing itself in the vehement breath which a wrathful man inhales and exhales.

Gill takes care over the direction of the jealousy: it is not against the people of God but against the enemy who had thought evil against them, and it is spoken in zeal for the divine glory and for the good of the people. Wesley says the same, and reads the great shaking as a disturbance and tumult like an earthquake. Gill argues from the shaking of the fishes of the sea that the commotion is not on account of the army or the devastations it shall make, but on account of the powerful presence of God, manifest in the destruction of that army. Ellicott generalises: the whole earth, animate and inanimate, is represented as affected by the terrible judgment of the Almighty upon his enemies, which is the common language of prophecy in describing great moral events and is especially used in connection with the judgments of the last day.

The sword called against the enemy is identified in three ways. Gill would rather render the particle as a causal one, following Noldius, so that the verse gives the reason for the commotion; and he takes the sword for the Christian kings whom God, having the swords of princes at his command, will call to the assistance of the Jews. Clarke names a particular commander who defeated the army of a Syrian king under his general, and observes against the rival identification that the king of Persia had no wars in the mountains of Israel. Wesley takes the sword for Israel itself, drawn from all parts of a land full of mountains, and compares an earlier slaughter in which every man drew on his brother.

The last judgments and the purpose are quickly told. Gill adds to the swords the pleading of God himself by his judgments, or, as the Targum has it, his taking vengeance, with a pestilence sent into the army such as destroyed the army of Sennacherib before Jerusalem. Clarke takes the hailstones and the fire and brimstone as probably figurative, signifying that the whole tide of the war should turn against the enemy, and reports Newcome supposing that the whole prophecy remains yet to be fulfilled, remarking that where such eminent scribes are divided none can decide. Gill closes on the purpose, that God shows the greatness of his power and the strictness of his justice and holiness in the destruction of the enemies of his people; Wesley, that he undeniably proves himself the mighty, just, faithful, wise, holy and merciful God, and declares himself true to his word.
